exercise.title: Why is the integral the limiting version of rate-times-width sums?

statement.p: The chapter began with distance as a sum of velocity times time, then area as a sum of height times width. In your own words, why is \int_a^b f(x)\,dx the same accumulation idea after the rectangles have been made infinitely thin?

hint.p: A Riemann sum is a finite estimate. The definite integral is the limit of those estimates.

note.title: What the project tests
note.p: An integral is not only an area under a drawn curve. It is accumulated rate. Power accumulates into energy, just as velocity accumulates into displacement.

exercise.title: Why must we keep signed accumulation distinct from total accumulation?

statement.p: Displacement integrates velocity; distance traveled integrates speed. In your own words, why is that distinction the chapter’s main interpretive warning, and what goes wrong if we treat every integral as ordinary geometric area?

hint.p: When f\ge0, the integral is ordinary area. When f changes sign, it measures positive accumulation minus negative accumulation.

exercise.title: Why does existence of an integral precede computing its value?

statement.p: Continuous functions, monotone functions, and functions with finitely many jumps are integrable; some bounded functions are not. In your own words, why must we know that the Riemann sums settle before we treat the integral as a number we can split, compare, or interpret?

hint.p: Properties assume the integral exists. The upper-lower test is what makes that assumption legitimate for the functions we actually use.

exercise.title: Why do the algebraic properties of the integral come from finite sums?

statement.p: Linearity, splitting over intervals, order, and symmetry all appeared first as habits of addition. In your own words, why should those rules be usable before we know many antiderivatives, and what does that say about where the integral’s arithmetic comes from?

hint.p: The integral was born from sums. Its basic properties are inherited from sums, then preserved by taking limits.
